requirements.statement: Offsetting exposures, such as a currency inflow and an equal outflow in the same period, form a natural hedge that reduces the firm's net risk, so separate hedges by individual units can be unnecessary at the enterprise level.

places.quote: exposures that offset each other are natural hedges, such as one division long and another short in the same currency, and hedging each separately wastes money
Hedging each division separately pays for two hedges that cancel each other, and leaves the company with a net hedge of the same €2 million it could have bought once.
Likewise a group with one division long a currency and another short the same currency does not need two hedges.

requirements.statement: External pressure as a force behind ERM is the demand from outside parties, such as regulators, rating agencies, and investors, that senior management take responsibility for enterprise-wide risk.

places.quote: Regulators, rating agencies, stock exchanges, institutional investors and corporate governance bodies came to insist that senior management take responsibility for managing risk across the whole enterprise.

requirements.statement: Quantification as a force behind ERM is the growing ability to measure risks using tools such as catastrophe models, financial models, and value at risk.

places.quote: Catastrophe modeling, which spread after Hurricane Andrew in 1992, and value at risk in banking made it easier to quantify risks, though operational and strategic risks remain hard to measure ([[Risk Measure]]).

requirements.statement: Boundaryless benchmarking as a force behind ERM is the sharing and comparison of risk management practices across organizations and industries.

places.quote: ERM tools and processes are shared across industries and countries, not confined to insurance.

requirements.statement: Traditional risk management grew out of corporate insurance buying, with the risk manager responsible for specific pure (hazard) risks, mainly by purchasing insurance and running loss control to protect employees and property.

places.quote: Risk management grew out of corporate insurance buying. The risk manager was responsible for specific pure risks, mainly by buying insurance and running loss control to keep employees and property safe, and typically reported to the treasurer.

places.quote: Risk management grew out of corporate insurance buying. The risk manager was responsible for specific pure risks, mainly by buying insurance and running loss control to keep employees and property safe, and typically reported to the treasurer.

requirements.statement: Enterprise risk management (ERM) treats hazard, financial, operational and strategic risks together as one portfolio, often overseen by a chief risk officer on the executive team.

places.quote: Larger organizations have a risk manager, and those practicing ERM a chief risk officer on the executive team.
Every [[Risk Taxonomies|category]] — insurance hazard, [[Financial Risk|financial]], [[Operational Risk|operational]] and strategic — is managed as one portfolio

requirements.statement: Setting enterprise-wide risk appetite and capital targets, with board oversight, is part of modern ERM governance rather than the traditional risk management role.

requirements.statement: The coefficient of variation of a random variable is its standard deviation divided by its mean (sigma/mu), a unitless measure of relative variability.

$CV$ is dimensionless, so it can compare the relative variability of distributions with different units or scales

places.quote: A larger $CV$ indicates greater dispersion relative to the mean

requirements.statement: Risk measures can be classified as solvency-related measures, which focus on the adverse tail of the outcome distribution, and performance-related measures, which focus on volatility around the mean.

The CAS's 2003 ERM overview splits ERM measures into *solvency-related* measures, which look at the adverse tail (probability of ruin, shortfall risk, VaR, EPD, TVaR) and concern customers and their proxies, regulators and rating agencies; and *performance-related* measures, which look at volatility near the mean (variance, standard deviation, semi-variance, below-target risk) and concern owners and their proxies, such as stock analysts.

requirements.statement: Probability of ruin is the probability that results fall far enough that capital is exhausted; it is a special case of shortfall risk and a solvency-related measure.

places.quote: *Solvency-related* measures look at the adverse tail of the distribution, such as the probability of ruin (the chance that capital is exhausted) and shortfall risk (the chance of falling below a threshold)

places.quote: [[Variance]] and [[Standard Deviation|standard deviation]] average the deviations from the mean, treating favourable and unfavourable surprises alike.

requirements.statement: Semi-variance measures variability using only unfavorable deviations below a target (such as plan or the mean), rather than the chance of capital exhaustion.

places.quote: *Semivariance* and downside standard deviation count only unfavourable deviations

requirements.statement: A speculative risk is a risk that offers the chance of a gain as well as a loss (e.g., launching a new product).

places.quote: A speculative risk offers a chance of gain as well as loss, such as an investment, a new product or a change in exchange rates.

places.quote: A pure risk offers only a chance of loss or no loss, such as fire, flood or a liability claim.
A pure risk offers a chance of loss and no chance of gain, such as physical damage to property from fire, flood or weather, liability claims, and natural disasters.
The exposure must offer only the chance of loss or no loss, as a fire or a theft does.

requirements.statement: Pure risks such as property damage, theft, and liability are the traditional subject of insurance, whereas enterprise risk management also considers speculative risks.

places.quote: Insurance deals mainly with pure risk ([[Insurable Risk]]), while [[Enterprise Risk Management|ERM]] considers pure and speculative risks together.
Traditional risk management and insurance deal with pure risk ([[Insurable Risk]]); [[Enterprise Risk Management|ERM]] considers both.

requirements.statement: A diversifiable (idiosyncratic) risk is one whose losses are independent across exposures, so pooling more exposures makes the average loss per exposure more predictable.

places.quote: A diversifiable, or idiosyncratic, risk is particular to one firm or exposure, so a large portfolio of independent exposures makes the loss per unit predictable
A diversifiable, or idiosyncratic, risk is particular to one firm or exposure, so holding many independent exposures makes the average loss predictable, as with fires at homes in different places.

places.quote: A nondiversifiable, or systemic, risk is shared by every exposure, so adding more does not reduce it: market risk, inflation and recession, regulatory and political risk.
A nondiversifiable, or systemic, risk is shared by every exposure, such as an economy-wide recession or inflation, and adding more exposures does not reduce it.

places.quote: A nondiversifiable, or systemic, risk is shared by every exposure, such as an economy-wide recession or inflation, and adding more exposures does not reduce it.
A nondiversifiable, or systemic, risk is shared by every exposure, so adding more does not reduce it: market risk, inflation and recession, regulatory and political risk.

requirements.statement: Perils that strike individual homes independently, such as kitchen fires and burglaries in different cities, are diversifiable: pooling more such exposures reduces the variability of loss per policy.

places.quote: A diversifiable, or idiosyncratic, risk is particular to one firm or exposure, so holding many independent exposures makes the average loss predictable, as with fires at homes in different places.
A diversifiable, or idiosyncratic, risk is particular to one firm or exposure, so a large portfolio of independent exposures makes the loss per unit predictable

places.quote: The complement rule is the workhorse shortcut — "at least one" is almost always faster as $1 - P(\text{none})$.

requirements.statement: Using a team with diverse perspectives to identify exposures raises the chance that an exposure is found compared with any single individual working alone.

places.quote: A cross-functional team brings operations, finance, legal, sales, IT and frontline staff together, because the people closest to a process know where it fails.
The team raises the chance of finding the exposure from 0.5 to 0.832, but only because its members see the business differently.

requirements.statement: Credit risk is the risk that a counterparty (such as a customer or borrower) fails to pay amounts owed, causing a loss to the firm.

places.quote: **Credit Risk** is the risk of loss because a counterparty fails to pay what it owes (**default**) or because its credit standing deteriorates, lowering the value of the claim before any default occurs.

places.quote: *credit risk* — bond issuers, [[Reinsurance Credit Risk|reinsurers]], agents and brokers, derivative counterparties;

requirements.statement: To identify risks from a balance sheet, examine each asset and liability item for how its value could be lost or impaired, and map it to the corresponding risk (e.g., receivables to customer nonpayment).

places.quote: Financial statements and accounting records point to exposures, since each asset on the balance sheet can be damaged or lost and each item of revenue or expense on the income statement can fall or rise.
The receivables point to credit risk if a grocery chain fails, a financial risk.

requirements.statement: Hazard risks are pure risks such as property damage and liability (e.g., product liability) that arise from physical assets or injuries and can only produce loss.

places.quote: **Hazard risks** come from fire and other property damage, windstorm and other natural perils, theft and other crime, personal injury, business interruption, disease and disability (including work-related injury) and liability claims.
A pure risk offers a chance of loss and no chance of gain, such as physical damage to property from fire, flood or weather, liability claims, and natural disasters.

requirements.statement: Reputational risk is a strategic risk concerning damage to the firm's standing with stakeholders.

places.quote: **Strategic** risks come from reputational damage, competition, customer wants, demographic and social trends, technological innovation, capital availability, and regulatory and political trends.

requirements.statement: A risk identification team finds more exposures when its members have diverse perspectives and knowledge of different parts of the organization, such as operations as well as finance.

places.quote: A cross-functional team brings operations, finance, legal, sales, IT and frontline staff together, because the people closest to a process know where it fails.
The value of a team comes from members who see different parts of the organization.

places.quote: A reviewer who shares the same sources and the same blind spots adds a person without adding a perspective.
Adding people from the same function, using the same documents, adds little.

requirements.statement: Operational staff such as maintenance personnel hold knowledge of equipment failures and operational hazards that financial documents do not show, making them a source of operational risk identification.

places.quote: Personal inspections of facilities and operations find hazards that documents never mention.
Expertise within the organization, such as plant managers and engineers, and beyond it, such as lawyers, consultants and insurers' risk control staff, fills in what the risk manager does not know.

requirements.statement: In group risk identification, a dominant senior voice can narrow the list of identified risks through deference and groupthink, a problem a facilitator must guard against.

places.quote: so that opinions converge without one dominant voice anchoring the rest.

requirements.statement: A risk map (heat map) plots each risk by its likelihood and impact on separate axes, showing where each risk sits rather than a single combined score.

places.quote: A risk map, or heat map, plots each risk by likelihood on one axis and impact on the other, with zones that mark which risks need action first.

requirements.statement: A risk score on ordinal scales is computed as likelihood rating multiplied by impact rating, so different likelihood-impact combinations can produce the same score.

places.quote: $S$ is a risk score, the product of a likelihood rating $\ell$ and an impact rating $m$, each usually on a scale of 1 to 5.
Vehicle accidents and the loss of the largest customer tie at 8, but they sit in different corners of the map.

requirements.statement: Ordinal ratings only rank risks; a product of ratings is not an expected loss in dollars, so score ratios do not give cost ratios.

places.quote: A score is a way to rank risks, not a measure of expected loss, since the scales are not proportional to probabilities or dollars.
Likelihood and impact ratings are ordinal, so a score of 12 is not twice as bad as a score of 6. Comparing scores as if they were dollars overstates their precision.

requirements.statement: High-frequency, low-severity risks are suited to retention combined with loss control, while low-frequency, high-severity risks are suited to risk transfer such as insurance.

places.quote: The traditional risk management matrix for one exposure points to retention for losses of low frequency and low severity, retention with loss control for high frequency and low severity, transfer by insurance for low frequency and high severity, and avoidance for high frequency and high severity.
a frequent small risk and a rare severe one can share a score but call for retention and control in the first case and transfer in the second.

requirements.statement: Equal risk scores do not imply equal treatment or priority, and a low product score does not make a severe, rare risk unimportant.

requirements.statement: Root cause analysis repeatedly asks why an event happened until reaching an underlying cause the organization can change, rather than stopping at the surface symptom.

places.quote: Root cause analysis works back from a loss or a near miss to the underlying cause, asking why it happened until the answer is something the organization can change.

requirements.statement: Probability analysis describes possible loss outcomes with a probability distribution and summarizes them with measures such as expected value; it does not trace causes.

places.quote: **Anticipate:** The organization scans its environment for threats and changes before they arrive

places.quote: **Adapt:** The organization changes how it works to fit the new conditions, by rerouting supply, changing products, moving staff or redesigning processes.

requirements.statement: The recover capability of resilience is returning operations to normal after a disruption through plans and resources.

places.quote: **Recover:** Plans and resources bring operations back to normal, or to a better new normal.

requirements.statement: Probable maximum loss (PML) is the largest loss expected to occur from a single event under probable (not absolute worst-case) conditions, such as the underwriter's judged maximum restoration period.

places.quote: An underwriter estimates the [[Probable Maximum Loss|probable maximum loss]] of business income as the income lost over the longest likely period of restoration, plus the extra expense the insured would incur.
Underwriters and loss control staff use probable maximum loss for one location: the largest loss expected there from a fire, stated in dollars or as a percentage of the location's total values.

Severity is also judged by the worst case: The Institutes distinguish the maximum possible loss, the total value exposed at one location or in one event, from the probable maximum loss, the largest loss likely to occur.

requirements.statement: For a seasonal business, the PML of business income is found by placing the restoration period at the worst-case timing, i.e., summing the highest-income consecutive months covering the restoration period, rather than using average monthly income.

places.quote: The worst case is a loss just before the peak season. Two 5-month windows give the largest income loss, August to December and September to January.

requirements.statement: Extra expense (costs incurred to continue operations after a loss) is added to the lost business income when computing the business income PML.

places.quote: An underwriter estimates the [[Probable Maximum Loss|probable maximum loss]] of business income as the income lost over the longest likely period of restoration, plus the extra expense the insured would incur.

requirements.statement: The period of restoration in business income coverage is the time needed to repair, rebuild, or replace the damaged property and resume operations; the maximum period of restoration is the longest such period for a loss.

places.quote: Its length is set by how long restoration should take, not by how long it actually takes or by the policy's expiration date, and an underwriter's estimate of its maximum length drives the probable maximum loss of [[Business Income Coverage|business income]].
It ends when the property should be repaired or replaced with reasonable speed, or when the business resumes at a new permanent location, and it is not cut short by the policy's expiration.

requirements.statement: The length of the period of restoration is driven by physical restoration factors such as building size and construction, permits and building codes, the season, and lead times for specialized machinery or equipment.

places.quote: A custom press, kiln or production line may have a lead time far longer than the building, and it often sets the critical path.
It depends on how long the property takes to rebuild, which grows with its size, its construction, building code and permit requirements and the season.

requirements.statement: Seasonality of sales affects the amount of income lost depending on when the loss occurs, not the time needed to restore the property.

places.quote: Weather can stop construction for part of the year, and a business that misses its peak season may lose most of a year's income even though restoration takes only months.
Seasonality is one of the main factors in the maximum loss during the period of restoration, and a business income limit sized on averages would be exhausted by a fire in late summer.

requirements.statement: Factors such as the ability to make up lost production after reopening reduce the size of the business income loss but do not shorten the period of restoration.

places.quote: It depends on how seasonal the business is and when the loss strikes, how much of its expense would continue, whether it can operate partially or move production to another site, whether lost production can be made up afterwards, and whether a single machine, process or supplier is a bottleneck.
